texto:
Viaplay Group completed the sale of its Dutch streaming and broadcasting operations to Videoland, the service owned by DPG Media, on October 30, 2026, for EUR 142 million (SEK 1.57 billion) on a cash and debt free basis. The Stockholm-listed group expects to keep about EUR 100 million (approximately SEK 1.1 billion) once transaction costs, restructuring costs and future payments on legacy multi-year agreements are settled, and said the money will go towards cutting its net debt.
In Short
Viaplay, a Nordic TV and streaming company, has finished selling its Dutch business to Videoland, a Dutch streaming service owned by DPG Media, for EUR 142 million. After paying the costs tied to the deal and to older contracts, Viaplay expects to keep about EUR 100 million, which it plans to use to pay down its debts. Viaplay now runs its own services only in the Nordic countries, and its former Dutch service is in the hands of the company that also owns RTL Nederland.
Four months from signing to closing
The agreement was made public on July 1, 2026. At the time, Viaplay said the sale needed approval from regulators and from its lenders, along with customary consents and procedures, and that it expected to close within months. When the group published its third-quarter report on October 22, the Dutch competition authority had already cleared the deal and Viaplay expected completion within weeks.
Closing came eight days later. The transaction "has received the required regulatory and lender approvals, and all other closing conditions have been fulfilled," according to Viaplay Group. From announcement to completion took 121 days, according to PPC Land's count.
Jørgen Madsen Lindemann, Viaplay Group's president and chief executive, framed the exit as a matter of focus. "Now that the transaction is complete, our resources are fully focused on our operations in our core Nordic markets, where we have the greatest scale and synergy potential," he said. "The proceeds will enable us to reduce net debt levels and strengthen our financial position as we continue our work to deliver increased profitability and positive cash flows."
He also addressed the staff who move with the business. "We are proud of the business we have built in the Netherlands, and grateful to our local colleagues for making this possible. We wish the team every success under the ownership of Videoland, which is well-placed locally to develop the business further."
From EUR 142 million to about EUR 100 million
The headline price sits slightly below the revenue of the business being sold. The Dutch operations generated net sales of EUR 149 million (approximately SEK 1.65 billion) in 2025, according to Viaplay Group. On PPC Land's calculation, the price equals about 0.95 times one year of sales. Neither the July nor the October announcement disclosed the unit's profit, its subscriber numbers or its headcount.
Not all of the EUR 142 million reaches Viaplay's bank account. Total cash proceeds are expected to amount to approximately EUR 100 million "after cash transaction costs, restructuring costs, and future payments in relation to legacy multi-year agreements," according to the company. That leaves a gap of roughly EUR 42 million, close to 30% of the headline figure, according to PPC Land's arithmetic. In kronor, the difference is about SEK 470 million.
How that EUR 42 million splits between the three categories is not stated. Nor does the announcement say which legacy agreements are involved, how long they run or whom the payments go to. The July announcement had referred more loosely to transaction and restructuring costs, "provisions" and balance sheet effects, without amounts. The closing announcement is the first time Viaplay has put a number on the cash it expects to keep.
Legacy contracts are a familiar cost for the group. In July, Viaplay put cash costs from legacy content agreements in non-core markets at about SEK 500 million for 2026, SEK 400 million for 2027 and SEK 200 million for 2028, all tied to markets the group has exited. In the third quarter alone, SEK 90 million went on legacy content agreements in markets Viaplay has already left. For the Netherlands, Viaplay has folded the equivalent commitments into its proceeds estimate. Whether those payments will be reported alongside the non-core legacy costs in future cash flow statements is not explained.
The accounting gain
The total net gain on the sale will include both the cash costs and non-cash balance sheet effects, and will be reported as items affecting comparability (IAC) in the fourth-quarter results, according to Viaplay Group. No estimate of the gain was given. That report is scheduled for February 18, 2027.
What the cash does to the debt
Viaplay carried net debt of SEK 5,418 million at the end of September, equal to 4.4 times trailing twelve-month pro forma EBITDA, excluding associated company income and items affecting comparability. Stripping out SEK 247 million of net lease liabilities, financial net debt was SEK 5,170 million. Of a SEK 2,817 million revolving credit facility, SEK 750 million was drawn, and aside from scheduled repayments all of the group's debt facilities mature in 2028.
Against that, SEK 1.1 billion is about one fifth of net debt. Applied in full, it would take the figure to roughly SEK 4.3 billion, according to PPC Land's calculation. The leverage ratio is harder to predict, because the earnings of the Dutch business leave the group too. On the third-quarter call on October 22, chief financial officer Johan Johansson declined to give figures for either the expected reduction in net debt or the EBITDA that would depart with the Dutch operations. The published numbers do not allow the post-sale ratio to be calculated.
The proceeds "will be used to reduce the Group's net debt level, and the Group will consider a refinancing of its outstanding borrowing facilities in due course, in order to reduce the Group's borrowing levels and costs," according to Viaplay Group. There is no timetable, no target amount and no indication of which facilities would be refinanced.
The expected SEK 1.1 billion is the same sum Viaplay agreed to pay for Telenor's 50% stake in Allente, the Nordic satellite and broadband provider it took full control of in November 2025. Lindemann linked the two deals in July, presenting the Dutch sale as the step that followed the Allente acquisition and the refinancing at the end of 2025.
Targets unchanged
The sale does not change the group's financial targets for 2026 or its long-term ambitions, both last set out in the third-quarter report, according to the company. Those targets call for core operation sales stable year on year on an organic basis and core operation EBITDA before associated company income and IAC of SEK 1.0 billion to SEK 1.4 billion, with SEK 871 million already booked after nine months. The longer-term ambition is a double-digit EBITDA margin in 2028. The Dutch business leaves the group with two months of the year still to run.
What Videoland takes over
The announcement describes the assets only as Viaplay's "Dutch streaming and broadcasting operations." It names no channels, sports rights or staff numbers, and it carries no comment from DPG Media or Videoland.
In April 2024, Viaplay Group announced a five-year Formula 1 agreement covering the Netherlands, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Norway and Iceland up to and including the 2029 season, with F1 TV Pro included in Dutch subscriptions, according to the group's announcement at the time. The same announcement listed Premier League and Bundesliga football and PDC darts in the Netherlands. So which of them moved to Videoland? Neither the July agreement nor the October closing statement says, and neither indicates whether the Dutch part of the Formula 1 contract is among the legacy agreements whose costs are netted from the proceeds.
The buyer already has scale in Dutch television. DPG Media completed its acquisition of RTL Nederland on July 1, 2025, and the Viaplay deal adds a second streaming and broadcasting business to the Belgian and Dutch media group within sixteen months. The July coverage noted that no timeline for rebranding or platform integration had been published, and the closing announcement does not add one. It is also silent on connected TV distribution arrangements such as the dedicated Viaplay button on Philips TVs running Titan OS, which covered the Netherlands as well as the Nordic countries.
Why the marketing community is watching
For advertisers and agencies, the closing narrows Viaplay to five markets: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. The group describes itself as running the Viaplay streaming service in every Nordic country, TV channels across most of its markets, commercial radio stations in Norway and Sweden, and the Viaplay Select content concept on partner platforms around the world. Apart from that licensing business, its consumer and advertising operations are now entirely Nordic.
That inventory is under pressure. In the third quarter, Viaplay's advertising sales fell 0.6% on an organic basis to SEK 766 million, as growth in digital formats failed to fully offset declining linear TV revenue. Advertising made up 15% of core operation net sales. Most of the remainder comes from subscriptions, split between the SVOD streaming service and non-streaming pay-TV packages that include Allente's satellite business.
The Nordic sports schedule is where Viaplay has kept spending. In February, it secured all EFL Championship rights in the Nordic countries until 2028, and in April it extended UEFA Champions League rights in Denmark through the 2030-31 season. Both are multi-year contracts in the Nordic markets where the group now says its resources are fully focused.
The deal also fits a wider pattern of European broadcasters consolidating as audiences move online. A survey by Boston Consulting Group and NativeResearch, released in September 2025, found that streaming platforms reached 97% of viewers and took 64% of weekly viewing time across the UK, France, Germany and Switzerland. At RTL Group, which sold its Dutch arm to DPG Media, TV advertising fell 4.0% to EUR 977 million in the first half of 2026 while digital advertising rose 10.9%. In the Netherlands, two broadcasting and streaming businesses that were separately owned two years ago now sit with one group.
What the sale will do for Viaplay's numbers is still open. The fourth-quarter report will show the size of the IAC gain, the actual cash received and the net debt after closing. Until then, the only firm figure is the approximately EUR 100 million Viaplay expects to keep from a business it sold for EUR 142 million.

- August 2026 - RTL Group reports first-half TV advertising down 4.0% to EUR 977 million and digital advertising up 10.9%

Summary
Who: Viaplay Group AB, the Nasdaq Stockholm-listed Nordic streaming and broadcasting group led by president and chief executive Jørgen Madsen Lindemann, and Videoland, the streaming service owned by DPG Media.
What: Viaplay completed the sale of its Dutch streaming and broadcasting operations to Videoland for EUR 142 million (SEK 1.57 billion) on a cash and debt free basis. The unit had 2025 net sales of EUR 149 million. Viaplay expects about EUR 100 million (approximately SEK 1.1 billion) in cash after transaction costs, restructuring costs and future payments on legacy multi-year agreements, will use it to reduce net debt and will consider refinancing its borrowing facilities. The net gain will be booked as items affecting comparability in the fourth quarter, and the 2026 targets are unchanged.
When: The sale was completed on October 30, 2026, 121 days after it was announced on July 1, 2026. The fourth-quarter report is scheduled for February 18, 2027.
Where: The Netherlands, where Viaplay no longer runs any services, and Viaplay's remaining markets of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden.
Why: Viaplay says the exit lets it focus resources on the Nordic markets where it has the greatest scale and synergy potential, and use the proceeds to cut net debt of SEK 5,418 million, which stood at 4.4 times trailing pro forma EBITDA at the end of September.
